title: WearSurfacesDatasets: how surfaces change as they wear

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Rub a piece of cardboard with sandpaper a little more each time, and scan it between rounds. After a while, you have a film of a surface slowly changing.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds a bit like a flipbook of damage.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is, and that's what WearSurfacesDatasets publishes. It's the public dataset from Antoine's master's research at ÉTS on wear in texture space: surface textures captured by a GelSight sensor during controlled wear tests, sorted by material, abrasive grit, load and sliding distance.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Graphics and tribology researchers who want real wear progressions. In the research, it's used to compare simulated wear patterns with measured microgeometry.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Each measured state stores several maps of the surface: height, normal, bump, displacement, ambient occlusion and hillshade. They come in two formats, Parquet files for browsing and WebDataset archives for streaming. The index lists twenty wear timelines.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Cardboard at five loads from ten to two hundred grams, foam, MDF with circle and line paths, PLA at several grits, soft wood, and unworn sandpaper references running from grit forty to two forty.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: But scans taken between rounds won't line up perfectly, will they?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's why the repository includes alignment tools. They register each sequence in two passes, crop the region all frames share, and can add in-between frames by interpolation. They can even extrapolate future normal maps with a model, though those are model output, not measurements.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And can I look at it without installing anything?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's a WebGPU viewer that reads the Parquet files right in the browser. You pick a sequence, load it, optionally align it, then scrub the sliding distance or press Play and watch the surface change.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's a time-lapse of wear you can scrub through.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. There are also command line tools to rebuild, extract and describe the dataset, and a PowerPoint deck for each test series. The scans come from the sliding bench shared in WearMachine, so the bench makes the wear and this dataset keeps it. The written page has the full layout of the data.
